title: Parallel Stochastic Gradient-Based Planning for World Models
claim: Successful plans must first move away from the goal, and baseline loss landscapes are rugged while ours is smooth.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: 2D line plot, then two 3D surfaces with shared colorbar
description: Three panels in a row. Panel (a) is a blue line plot of MSE similarity loss against time step (0 to 50). It drops sharply from 1.0 to about 0.4, rises to about 0.7 around step 20-25, then falls to 0 at the end. Small boxed insets mark the 'start' and 'goal' Push-T block configurations. Panels (b) and (c) are 3D surface plots of loss over two random action-space directions, drawn in a viridis colormap (purple is low loss, yellow is high). The GD landscape in (b) is jagged, with many spikes and valleys. Our landscape in (c) is a smooth, gently sloped bowl. A vertical colorbar labeled 'loss' sits between (b) and (c). Captions sit below each panel. The eye goes first to the contrast between the rugged and smooth surfaces.
caption: Difficulty of the planning problem. Subfigure (a) shows the distance to the goal in L2 norm throughout a successful trajectory. This illustrates the difficulty of planning optimization away from a minimizer: successful trajectories often have to first move away from the goal to successfully plan towards it later, resulting in greedy strategies failing. Subfigures (b)-(c) depict the loss landscape at convergence of standard rollout-based planners vs. our planner. The example given is in the Push-T environment at horizon length 50. The axes plotted over are with respect to two random, orthogonal, unit-norm directions in the full action space R50×2. Our planner loss is taken as in Eq. (10), and for GD the loss is taken as in Eq. (3).
abstract: World models simulate environment dynamics from raw sensory inputs like video. However, using them for planning can be challenging due to the vast and unstructured search space. We propose a robust and highly parallelizable planner that leverages the differentiability of the learned world model for efficient optimization, solving long-horizon control tasks from visual input. Our method treats states as optimization variables ("virtual states") with soft dynamics constraints, enabling parallel computation and easier optimization. To facilitate exploration and avoid local optima, we introduce stochasticity into the states. To mitigate sensitive gradients through high-dimensional vision-based world models, we modify the gradient structure to descend towards valid plans while only requiring action-input gradients. Our planner, which we call GRASP (Gradient RelAxed Stochastic Planner), can be viewed as a stochastic version of a non-condensed or collocation-based optimal controller. We provide theoretical justification and experiments on video-based world models, where our resulting planner outperforms existing planning algorithms like the cross-entropy method (CEM) and vanilla gradient-based optimization (GD) on long-horizon experiments, both in success rate and time to convergence.
